title: History Stories
intro_zh: 19 篇历史短文，讲述中国与世界历史上的人物与事件。
intro_en: 19 short history readings about people and events in China and the world.

chapters.title: The Wright Brothers and the First Flight
chapters.body: Over a hundred years ago, two brothers owned a small bicycle shop. Wilbur and Orville Wright loved machines and spent their free time studying how birds fly. They watched how a bird tilts its wings to turn, and they decided to build a flying machine of their own. They fixed a small propeller to the front of the machine and laid a long wooden runway on the sand. They tested many models on the beach, where the wind was strong and steady. Each test taught them something new, and they often failed before they succeeded. On a cold December morning in 1903, their plane was ready. Orville lay on the lower wing while Wilbur ran beside it. The engine started, and the plane climbed to a low altitude above the waves. A sudden gust of wind pushed against the wings, but the plane held steady. It stayed up for only twelve seconds and traveled about forty meters. But those twelve seconds changed the world. Today, huge planes carry people across oceans, and it all began with two careful brothers and a wooden machine on a windy beach.

quizzes.question: What did the Wright brothers own before building planes?
quizzes.explanation_zh: 莱特兄弟原来开着一家自行车店。
quizzes.explanation_en: The Wright brothers owned a bicycle shop before building planes.

quizzes.question: What helped them learn how birds turn?

options.text: Watching a bird tilt its wings

quizzes.explanation_zh: 他们观察鸟如何倾斜翅膀来转弯，从中得到灵感。
quizzes.explanation_en: They watched a bird tilt its wings to turn, which gave them the idea.

quizzes.question: How long was the first successful flight?
quizzes.explanation_zh: 首次飞行只持续了约 12 秒、飞了约 40 米，却改变了世界。
quizzes.explanation_en: The first flight lasted only about twelve seconds and covered about 40 meters, yet it changed the world.

chapters.title: How Paper Was Invented
chapters.body: A long time ago, people wrote on bamboo, silk, and animal skin. These materials were heavy or very expensive. Around two thousand years ago, a man named Cai Lun wanted to make a lighter and cheaper writing surface. He watched how cloth makers pressed wet fibers into thin sheets. He tried many things, such as tree bark, old cloth, and fishing nets. He broke these materials into tiny pieces and soaked them in water. Then he pressed the wet mixture into flat sheets and left them to dry. The result was light, smooth, and easy to write on. Paper had arrived. Soon people used it everywhere, and the knowledge spread to many countries. Paper made books lighter and learning easier. The next time you turn a page, remember the patient man who turned old rags and bark into something the whole world still uses every day.

quizzes.question: What did people write on before paper?
quizzes.explanation_zh: 纸发明前，人们写在竹简、丝绸和兽皮上，又重又贵。
quizzes.explanation_en: Before paper, people wrote on bamboo, silk, and animal skin — heavy and expensive.

quizzes.question: Who wanted to make a lighter, cheaper writing surface?
quizzes.explanation_zh: 约两千年前，一个叫蔡伦的人想做出更轻更便宜的书写材料。
quizzes.explanation_en: About two thousand years ago, a man named Cai Lun wanted a lighter and cheaper writing surface.

quizzes.question: Which of these did Cai Lun use to make paper?

options.text: Tree bark, old cloth, and fishing nets

quizzes.explanation_zh: 蔡伦尝试用树皮、旧布、渔网等材料造纸。
quizzes.explanation_en: Cai Lun made paper from tree bark, old cloth, and fishing nets.

chapters.title: The Origins of Month Names: Marks of Roman Mythology and History
chapters.title_zh: 月份名字的由来：罗马神话与历史印记
chapters.subtitle: 各个月份名字的来历：古罗马神话与历史的印记
chapters.body: Have you ever wondered why January comes first, or why September means the ninth month even though its name sounds like "seven"? The names of our twelve months come mostly from ancient Rome, blending gods, emperors, and old Roman numbers. In the early Roman calendar, the year had only 10 months and began in March. January (Janus) is named after the Roman god of gates, beginnings, and transitions, who had two faces looking forward and backward. February comes from februa, an ancient Roman festival of purification. March honors Mars, the Roman god of war. April likely comes from a Latin word meaning "to open," celebrating flowers opening in spring. May is named after Maia, the goddess of growth and spring, while June honors Juno, the queen of the gods. The later months carry numbers from the old Roman calendar. September comes from septem (seven), October from octo (eight), November from novem (nine), and December from decem (ten). Even though Julius Caesar and Augustus added January and February to the start of the year—shifting the numbered months to positions 9 through 12—their original names stayed the same! Finally, the summer months immortalize two powerful Roman rulers. July is named after Julius Caesar, who reformed the calendar, and August is named after his adopted son Augustus, the first Roman emperor. Every time we check a calendar, we are reading a story thousands of years old!

quizzes.question: Which Roman god is January named after

options.text: Janus, the god of beginnings and transitions.

quizzes.explanation_zh: January 名字来源于罗马神话中掌管门、开始和过渡的双面神雅努斯 Janus
quizzes.explanation_en: Janus, the god of beginnings and transitions.

quizzes.question: Why do months like September and October have names that mean "seven" and "eight" even though they are months 9 and 10

options.text: Because ancient Romans could not count past eight.
Because they were originally named under an old Roman calendar that started in March with 10 months.
Because the spelling changed by mistake in modern times.

quizzes.explanation_zh: 早期罗马历法只有10个月且从3月开始，因此 September 和 October 保留了旧历法中的数字词根
quizzes.explanation_en: Because they were originally named under an old Roman calendar that started in March with 10 months.

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) The months of July and August are named after famous Roman rulers, Julius Caesar and Augustus.
quizzes.explanation_zh: July 纪念尤利乌斯·恺撒，August 纪念第一位罗马皇帝奥古斯都
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) The months of July and August are named after famous Roman rulers, Julius Caesar and Augustus.

chapters.title: The Origins of Weekday Names
chapters.subtitle: 星期名字的来历
chapters.body: Have you ever wondered why we have a seven-day week? The tradition comes from ancient Babylon and Rome, where people named the days after celestial bodies (the sun, the moon, and the five visible planets) and their gods. In English, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday are named after Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon. Tuesday through Friday honor ancient Norse mythology gods: Tiw (god of war), Woden, Thor (the thunder god), and Freya (goddess of love). In Japanese, the names of the days are fascinating because they combine astronomy with Chinese philosophy, known as the "Seven Luminaries" (七曜). Japanese days use the sun, moon, and the five natural elements: Fire (Tuesday, associated with Mars), Water (Wednesday, associated with Mercury), Wood (Thursday, associated with Jupiter), Gold/Metal (Friday, associated with Venus), and Earth (Saturday, associated with Saturn). For example, Monday is Getsuyoubi (Moon day), and Tuesday is Kayoubi (Fire day). Different cultures also disagree on which day the week begins! In many Western countries like the United States, calendars start the week on Sunday, which has religious roots as a day of rest and worship. However, according to the ISO standard (international standard) and in countries like China and most of Europe, Monday is officially the first day of the week because it marks the beginning of the school and work week. Meanwhile, in many Islamic countries, the week starts on Saturday or Sunday. No matter when your week starts, every day has a rich and ancient story behind it!

quizzes.question: What are English weekday names like Saturday, Sunday, and Monday originally based on
quizzes.explanation_zh: 文中指出英文星期名称源于天体以及古罗马或北欧神话中的神祇
quizzes.explanation_en: Celestial bodies and ancient gods.

quizzes.question: In the Japanese naming system for days, what does Wednesday represent
quizzes.explanation_zh: 日语中星期三对应水曜日，与水星和水元素相关
quizzes.explanation_en: Water (associated with Mercury).

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) In international standards and countries like China, Monday is officially treated as the first day of the week.
quizzes.explanation_zh: 根据国际标准（ISO）以及中国和欧洲大部分地区，星期一被定为一周的第一天
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) In international standards and countries like China, Monday is officially treated as the first day of the week.

chapters.title: Why Do Months Have Different Numbers of Days? Roman Politics and Superstitions
chapters.subtitle: 为什么每个月的天数不一样？古罗马的政治与迷信

terms.bad luck: 运气不佳; 晦气; 灾星; 恶运
terms.named after: na. name for 用(别人,别物的名字)命名

chapters.body: Have you ever wondered why some months have 30 days, others have 31, and February has only 28 (or 29 in a leap year)? The strange lengths of our months are not based on science or the moon; instead, they are the result of ancient Roman history, politics, and ancient superstitions! In the earliest Roman calendar, the year had only 10 months and lasted 304 days, leaving winter as an uncounted gap. Around 700 BCE, a king named Numa Pompilius added January and February to cover the winter and make a 12-month year of 355 days. At that time, Romans had a strange superstition: they believed that even numbers brought bad luck! Because of this, Numa tried to make all months have odd numbers of days (either 29 or 31). However, math got in the way. To make the total days add up to 355, one month had to have an even number. They chose February, the final month of the year dedicated to purification (februa ), giving it 28 days. People thought bad luck wouldn't matter much in a short, purifying month! Centuries later, Julius Caesar introduced a new calendar (the Julian calendar ) to match the sun's 365-day cycle. He added days to make most months 30 or 31 days long. Later, his successor Augustus named August after himself. Legend says Augustus did not want his month to be shorter than July (named after Julius Caesar), so he stole a day from February and added it to August, locking February into its short 28-day shape forever!

quizzes.question: Why did ancient Romans originally try to give most months odd numbers of days

options.text: Because odd numbers matched the phases of the moon.
Because they believed even numbers brought bad luck.
Because the sun only shines on odd days.

quizzes.explanation_zh: 古罗马人迷信偶数会带来厄运，因此尽量让大多数月份拥有奇数天数
quizzes.explanation_en: Because they believed even numbers brought bad luck.

quizzes.question: Which month was chosen to have 28 days because it was a time of purification and bad luck didn't matter as much
quizzes.explanation_zh: 文中指出二月是用于净化的月份，因此被赋予了28天的偶数天数
quizzes.explanation_en: February

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) Emperor Augustus took a day from February so his month (August) would not be shorter than Julius Caesar's month (July).
quizzes.explanation_zh: 传说奥古斯都为了让自己的月份 August 和恺撒的 July 一样长，从二月偷走了一天
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) Emperor Augustus took a day from February so his month (August) would not be shorter than Julius Caesar's month (July).

chapters.title: Xu Xiake: A Legendary Traveler Measuring China on Foot
chapters.title_zh: 徐霞客：用双脚丈量中国
chapters.subtitle: 徐霞客：用双脚丈量华夏大地的千古奇人
chapters.body: Xu Xiake (1587–1641) was a legendary geographer, traveler, and writer during the late Ming Dynasty. Unlike standard scholar-officials of his time who spent their lives studying for civil service exams, Xu chose a different path: traveling across China for over thirty years to explore mountains, rivers, and mysterious caves. Driven by curiosity, Xu covered thousands of miles across dozens of modern Chinese provinces, traveling mostly on foot. His extraordinary life was dedicated to scientific field study, which he documented in detail in his famous masterwork, The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake His contributions to geography were groundbreaking. He was the world's first pioneer to systematically study and document karst landforms (limestone formations), describing underground caves and subterranean rivers centuries before Western scientists. He also accurately identified the true source of the Yangtze River—the Jinsha River —correcting ancient geographic errors that had lasted for over a thousand years. However, historical evaluations also note certain limitations and negative aspects. Living in a feudal society, Xu relied on private servants, mountain carriers, and local officials during his long journeys. Historical records show that on some arduous trips, his heavy demands placed severe burdens on local villagers and porters. Furthermore, his research was mostly limited to qualitative observation without using modern scientific tools or quantitative measurements. Despite these historical limitations, Xu Xiake is widely celebrated as the father of Chinese travel writing and geography. Today, May 19th (the day he began his diaries) is officially designated as China Tourism Day, and many roads, parks, and landmarks across China—such as Xu Xiake Town in Jiangsu Province—are named after him to honor his incredible spirit of exploration!

quizzes.question: What major scientific discovery did Xu Xiake make regarding the Yangtze River

options.text: He proved that the Jinsha River is the true source of the Yangtze River.
He built the first bridge over the Yangtze River.

quizzes.explanation_zh: 徐霞客纠正了上千年的历史错误，考察确认金沙江才是长江的真正源头
quizzes.explanation_en: He proved that the Jinsha River is the true source of the Yangtze River.

quizzes.question: Which unique geological feature was Xu Xiake the world's first to systematically document
quizzes.explanation_zh: 文中指他是世界上最早系统考察和记录喀斯特地貌及地下溶洞的先驱
quizzes.explanation_en: Karst landforms and underground caves

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) Despite historical limitations, Xu Xiake's achievements are so widely recognized that places like Xu Xiake Town are named in his honor.
quizzes.explanation_zh: 尽管存在时代局限性，但他依然广受尊敬，中国许多地方如徐霞客镇均以他的名字命名
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) Despite historical limitations, Xu Xiake's achievements are so widely recognized that places like Xu Xiake Town are named in his honor.

chapters.title: The Four Great Classic Novels of China: Ancient Epics and Modern Legends
chapters.title_zh: 中国四大名著：古代史诗与传奇
chapters.subtitle: 中国四大古典名著：流传千古的东方史诗与现代传奇
chapters.body: China's "Four Great Classic Novels" are the most celebrated masterpieces in Chinese literature. Written over hundreds of years, they offer a deep window into Chinese history, philosophy, and society. Here is the four-novel collection arranged by the estimated time of writing Romance of the Three Kingdoms (Written in the 14th century, early Ming Dynasty) Luo Guanzhong (罗贯中). Set during the turbulent fall of the Han Dynasty, this grand historical epic chronicles the power struggles, brilliant military strategies, and heroics among three warring kingdoms: Wei, Shu, and Wu. Water Margin (Written in the 14th century, early-to-mid Ming Dynasty) Shi Nai'an (施耐庵). Set in the Song Dynasty, the story follows a band of 108 outlaws who gather at Mount Liang (Liangshan Marsh) to rebel against corrupt government officials and fight for justice. Journey to the West (Written in the 16th century, late Ming Dynasty) Wu Chengen (吴承恩). A thrilling mythological fantasy following the Buddhist monk Tang Sanzang and his three magical disciples—including the legendary Sun Wukong (the Monkey King)—on an epic quest to retrieve sacred scriptures from India. Dream of the Red Chamber (Written in the 18th century, middle Qing Dynasty) Written by Cao Xueqin (曹雪芹). A deeply moving masterpiece centered on the romantic tragedy between Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu, recording the rise and tragic fall of a wealthy noble family in feudal China. Today, these four masterpieces enjoy massive modern influence. Classic TV shows adapted from them have been rewatched billions of times across Asia. Furthermore, they are a endless source of inspiration for video games worldwide—from tactical games like Total War: Three Kingdoms to action blockbusters like Black Myth: Wukong, bringing these ancient tales to life for a global audience!

quizzes.question: Which novel is estimated to have been written first among the Four Great Classics
quizzes.explanation_zh: 文中按撰写年代排列，约写于14世纪明初的《三国演义》成书最早
quizzes.explanation_en: Romance of the Three Kingdoms

quizzes.question: Who is the estimated author of Journey to the West
quizzes.explanation_zh: 《西游记》推测的作者是吴承恩
quizzes.explanation_en: Wu Chengen

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) Modern video games like Black Myth: Wukong show the lasting influence of classic Chinese literature in global pop culture.
quizzes.explanation_zh: 像《黑神话：悟空》这样的现代化游戏展示了四大名著在现代流行文化中的巨大影响力
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) Modern video games like Black Myth: Wukong show the lasting influence of classic Chinese literature in global pop culture.

chapters.title: Master Xuanzang's Pilgrimage: The Real Legend and Differences from the Novel
chapters.subtitle: 玄奘取经：真实的西行传奇与《西游记》的差异
chapters.body: When people hear the name Xuanzang (玄奘), they often think of the sensitive monk protected by magical disciples in the famous novel Journey to the West. However, the real history behind Master Xuanzang is far more courageous, dramatic, and inspiring than any fictional tale! Xuanzang was his dharma name (monk name), while his lay name (birth name) was Chen Hui (陈祎). Disappointed by incomplete and contradictory Buddhist translations in China, he made a brave decision: to travel to India himself to collect original Sanskrit scriptures. Because the Tang government was at war, traveling abroad was banned. Xuanzang actually smuggled himself out of China, embarking on his dangerous journey in secret as a fugitive! The real Xuanzang was not a weak man saved by Monkey Kings; he was a tall, fearless scholar with an iron will. He crossed blistering deserts and icy mountains alone, nearly dying of thirst and escaping bandits multiple times. After reaching India, he spent many years studying at Nalanda Temple, the world's highest center of Buddhist learning. Xuanzang became a master of philosophy and won high praise in India after defeating top scholars in grand theological debates Xuanzang's far-reaching legacy profoundly shaped East Asian culture. He returned to China with hundreds of precious scriptures, spending the rest of his life translating millions of words with unmatched precision. His detailed travel record, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, provided rare geographical and historical data that modern archaeologists used centuries later to rediscover ancient sites across India and Central Asia. He remains one of the greatest cultural bridges in human history!

quizzes.question: What was Master Xuanzang's lay name (birth name) before becoming a monk
quizzes.explanation_zh: 玄奘的俗名/本名是陈祎 Chen Hui
quizzes.explanation_en: Chen Hui

quizzes.question: How did Xuanzang initially leave Tang Dynasty China for India

options.text: He was sent as an official ambassador by the Emperor.
He bought an official airline ticket.
He smuggled himself out secretly because traveling abroad was banned.

quizzes.explanation_zh: 文中指出当时唐朝禁止出境，玄奘是以“偷渡”的方式偷偷离开国境的
quizzes.explanation_en: He smuggled himself out secretly because traveling abroad was banned.

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) Modern archaeologists have used Xuanzang's book, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, to locate and rediscover lost ancient sites in India and Central Asia.
quizzes.explanation_zh: 玄奘撰写的《大唐西域记》为后世考古学家重新发现印度和中亚的古迹提供了极具价值的历史地理依据
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) Modern archaeologists have used Xuanzang's book, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, to locate and rediscover lost ancient sites in India and Central Asia.

chapters.title: Jianzhen's Voyages to Japan: Six Trials and a Bridge of Cultural Exchange
chapters.title_zh: 鉴真东渡：六次磨难与文化之桥
chapters.subtitle: 鉴真东渡：六折不挠的弘法传奇与中日文化桥梁
chapters.body: Jianzhen (688–763) was a high-ranking Buddhist monk of the Tang Dynasty whose unwavering determination left a legendary mark on East Asian history. In the 8th century, Japanese monks traveled to China to invite a master who could establish proper Buddhist ordination rules in Japan. Master Jianzhen accepted the challenging mission, declaring that he would sacrifice his life for the sake of the Dharma. Accomplishing this journey was extraordinarily dangerous. Crossing the stormy East China Sea in small wooden ships meant facing deadly typhoons, shipwrecks, and pirate attacks. Jianzhen attempted the voyage five times, all ending in failure. During his fifth attempt, his ship was blown far south to Hainan Island, and on the long return journey north, he suffered a severe illness and lost his eyesight completely. Despite being blind and in his sixties, Master Jianzhen never gave up. On his sixth attempt in 753, he finally landed safely in Japan! Emperor Shōmu and Japanese monks welcomed him with grand respect. Jianzhen built the famous Tōshōdai-ji temple in Nara and established the official Buddhist ordination system in Japan. Jianzhen brought much more than religious teachings; he brought a treasure trove of Chinese civilization. Accompanied by craftsmen, doctors, and artists, he introduced advanced Tang Dynasty architecture, sculpture, medicine, and calligraphy to Japan. He cured illnesses using Chinese herbal medicine and shaped Japanese culture so deeply that he is still honored in Japan today as the "Father of Japanese Medicine" and a supreme cultural ambassador.

quizzes.question: How many times did Master Jianzhen attempt to sail to Japan before he finally succeeded
quizzes.explanation_zh: 文中指出鉴真历经五次失败，在第六次东渡时才成功到达日本
quizzes.explanation_en: Six times

quizzes.question: What severe hardship did Master Jianzhen suffer before his successful final voyage

options.text: He was imprisoned for twenty years.
He lost his eyesight and became blind.

quizzes.explanation_zh: 鉴真在第五次东渡失败回程途中不幸双目失明
quizzes.explanation_en: He lost his eyesight and became blind.

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) Besides Buddhist teachings, Master Jianzhen also introduced advanced Chinese medicine, architecture, and calligraphy to Japan.
quizzes.explanation_zh: 鉴真不仅传播佛法，还将唐朝的建筑、雕塑、医药和书法带到了日本
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) Besides Buddhist teachings, Master Jianzhen also introduced advanced Chinese medicine, architecture, and calligraphy to Japan.

chapters.title: Martin Luther King Jr.: Civil Rights Giant and "I Have a Dream"
chapters.subtitle: 马丁·路德·金：民权巨擘与“我有一个梦想”

terms.political leader: 政治领袖；政治领导；政治领导人
terms.nonviolent resistance: n. 非暴力（主义），非暴力抵抗
terms.rose to: un. 出人头地；在世界上爬上去；满足；对…应付自如；出人头地；在社会大显身手；应付；发迹
terms.lives on: na. 以…为主食；靠…生活；继续活着；靠［吃］…生活

chapters.body: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a visionary American minister, activist, and political leader who became the most prominent spokesperson of the Civil Rights Movement. Inspired by his Christian faith and Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of nonviolent resistance, Dr. King led a courageous struggle against racial segregation and injustice across the United States. Born in Atlanta, Georgia, Dr. King rose to national leadership during the 1955 Montgomery Bus Boycott, which successfully ended segregated seating on public buses. Over the next decade, he organized nonviolent marches, sit-ins, and protests against systemic racism. Despite facing constant threats, arrests, and violence, he remained committed to peaceful change. In 1964, at age 35, he became the youngest person at the time to receive the Nobel Peace Prize On August 28, 1963, Dr. King delivered his historic "I Have a Dream" speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., before a crowd of over 250,000 people. His speech became an iconic rallying cry for freedom and human dignity. Among its most famous passages is his timeless hope for future generations: "I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character." Tragically, Dr. King was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1968, but his legacy lives on. His leadership paved the way for landmark federal legislation, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, forever altering the course of American history.

quizzes.question: What core principle did Dr. King adopt from Mahatma Gandhi to fight racial segregation
quizzes.explanation_zh: 马丁·路德·金受甘地哲学启发，坚持采用非暴力抗争的方式争取民权
quizzes.explanation_en: Nonviolent resistance

quizzes.question: According to Dr. King's famous quote, how did he hope his children would be judged in the future

options.text: By their wealth and family background
By the color of their skin
By the content of their character

quizzes.explanation_zh: 名言中明确表达希望人们来评价他的孩子们
quizzes.explanation_en: 不以肤色，而是以品格的优劣

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? (True or False) Dr. King delivered his iconic "I Have a Dream" speech at the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington in 1963.
quizzes.explanation_zh: 1963年8月28日，他在华盛顿林肯纪念堂前发表了著名的《我有一个梦想》演讲
quizzes.explanation_en: (True or False) Dr. King delivered his iconic "I Have a Dream" speech at the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington in 1963.

chapters.title_zh: 马丁·路德·金：我有一个梦想

chapters.title: The American Revolutionary War: The Birth of Freedom and Global Repercussions
chapters.title_zh: 美国独立战争：自由的诞生
chapters.subtitle: 美国独立战争：自由的诞生与世界的震荡
chapters.body: The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) was a historic conflict in which thirteen British colonies in North America fought for and won their independence from Great Britain, giving birth to a new nation: the United States of America. The primary causes of the war boiled down to economic oppression and political rights. Following the expensive Seven Years' War, the British Parliament imposed heavy taxes on the American colonies—such as the Stamp Act and the Tea Act—without granting them representation in Parliament. Outraged colonists rallied around the famous slogan: "No taxation without representation!" Tensions escalated into protests like the Boston Tea Party in 1773, prompting harsh British crackdowns. In 1775, fighting erupted at the Battles of Lexington and Concord. The following year, on July 4, 1776, the Second Continental Congress issued the historic Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson. Led by Commander-in-Chief George Washington, the Continental Army faced harsh winters, severe supply shortages, and untrained troops. However, turning points like the Battle of Saratoga convinced France and Spain to enter the war as allies, providing critical naval and financial support. In 1781, combined American and French forces trapped the main British army at the Siege of Yorktown, forcing their surrender. The war reached its official outcome with the signing of the Treaty of Paris in 1783, in which Great Britain recognized the independence and borders of the United States. The far-reaching impact of the war reshaped world history. Domestically, it led to the drafting of the U.S. Constitution and the creation of a modern federal republic. Globally, its ideals of liberty, democracy, and popular sovereignty inspired the French Revolution in 1789 and independence movements across Latin America, proving that a colony could break free from a global empire.

chapters.title: The Turbulent French Revolution: From Enlightenment to the Republic
chapters.title_zh: 动荡法国大革命：从启蒙到共和
chapters.subtitle: 法国大革命的曲折史诗：从启蒙曙光到共和确立
chapters.body: The French Revolution is one of the most complex and dramatic transformations in human history. Far from a smooth march toward liberty, it was a century-long roller coaster of radical ideals, violence, imperial conquests, and monarchical restorations. In the 18th century, the Enlightenment laid the intellectual foundation for change. Thinkers like Voltaire, Rousseau, and Montesquieu challenged divine right, advocating for liberty, equality, and popular sovereignty. Facing financial bankruptcy, King Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General in 1789—a assembly representing the clergy (First Estate), nobility (Second Estate), and commoners (Third Estate). When the Third Estate was outvoted, they broke away to form the National Assembly, sparking the outbreak of the Revolution with the storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789. The revolutionary process quickly descended into radicalism. Threatening foreign invasions and domestic counter-revolutions gave rise to extremism. Led by Robespierre and the Jacobins, the "Reign of Terror" executed tens of thousands by guillotine, including the King and Queen. This period proved the extreme dangers of fanaticism, showing how noble ideals of liberty can easily turn into brutal tyranny when unchecked by law and human rights. Out of the political chaos emerged Napoleon Bonaparte. Seizing power in 1799, he crowned himself Emperor, codified civil law with the Napoleonic Code, and conquered much of continental Europe before his eventual defeat at Waterloo in 1815. What followed was a turbulent cycle: the Bourbon Restoration brought back absolute monarchs, leading to the 1848 revolution and the rise of Napoleon III (Second Empire). In 1871, following France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, the working-class uprising known as the Paris Commune briefly seized the capital before being brutally suppressed. Finally, out of these ashes, the Third Republic stably emerged. France's repeated street protests and regime changes earned it the affectionate modern nickname "the capital of revolution" (革命老区). The legacy of this winding path is profound: it permanently destroyed feudalism in Western Europe, spread modern republicanism, and deeply influenced international relations—including shaping American politics as early political parties clashed over supporting French radicalism versus British stability.

chapters.title: The Rosetta Stone: Unlocking the Legend of Ancient Egypt
chapters.title_zh: 罗塞塔石碑：破解古埃及传奇
chapters.subtitle: 罗塞塔石碑：解锁古埃及文明的破译传奇
chapters.body: For over a thousand years, the mysterious picture-writing of ancient Egypt—known as hieroglyphics —remained a complete riddle to the world. Nobody living could read the secrets carved into tomb walls or papyrus scrolls. That all changed with the extraordinary discovery and decoding of a single slab of dark granodiorite: the Rosetta Stone In 1799, during Napoleon Bonaparte's military campaign in Egypt, French soldiers building a fort near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) uncovered a massive broken stone. The stone was unique because it featured the exact same decree—issued in 196 BCE by King Ptolemy V—carved in three distinct scripts Hieroglyphics: The sacred script used for official and religious documents. Demotic: The everyday cursive script used by ordinary Egyptian people. Ancient Greek: The official language of the ruling Greek administration in Egypt. Because scholars could still read Ancient Greek, they realized the stone provided a direct translation key! The race to decipher the Egyptian scripts began, becoming a battle of intellects between English polymath Thomas Young and French linguist Jean-François Champollion. Young made a crucial breakthrough by realizing that the oval rings—called cartouches —contained the phonetic spellings of royal names like "Ptolemy." In 1822, Champollion achieved the ultimate breakthrough. He proved that hieroglyphics were not merely symbolic picture-puzzles, but a complex combination of phonetic sounds (letters/syllables) and logograms (words/ideas). By cracking the code, Champollion reopened the door to three thousand years of Egyptian history, allowing modern historians to finally read ancient texts directly! Today, the Rosetta Stone remains the centerpiece of the British Museum and a universal symbol of translation and discovery.

chapters.title: The Louvre Museum: A Temple of Art
chapters.subtitle: 卢浮宫博物馆：艺术的殿堂
chapters.body: Located in the heart of Paris along the Seine River, the Louvre Museum is the world's largest and most visited art museum. Housed in the grand Louvre Palace—originally built as a medieval fortress in the late 12th century—the building served as a royal residence for centuries before opening as a public museum during the French Revolution in 1793. Today, its vast collections span thousands of years, housing world-famous masterpieces such as the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo, and the Winged Victory of Samothrace Standing in stark, brilliant contrast to the museum's historic classical architecture is the iconic Louvre Pyramid, located in the central courtyard (Cour Napoléon). Unveiled in 1989 as part of France's Grand Louvre project, this massive structure made of glass and metal serves as the museum's main underground entrance, improving visitor flow while flooding the subterranean lobby with natural sunlight. The famous pyramid was designed by the world-renowned Chinese-American architect

chapters.title: The Panthéon: Resting Place of Giants
chapters.title_zh: 法国先贤祠：巨擘的归宿
chapters.subtitle: 法国先贤祠：巨擘的归宿
chapters.body: Located on the Left Bank of Paris in the historic Latin Quarter, the Panthéon is a striking monument dedicated to honoring the greatest figures in French history. Its grand facade bears the famous inscription: "Aux grands hommes, la patrie reconnaissante" —"To great men, the grateful homeland." The building was originally commissioned by King Louis XV around 1758 as a magnificent church dedicated to Saint Genevieve, the patron saint of Paris. However, by the time construction was completed during the outbreak of the French Revolution in 1791, the Revolutionary government decided to transform the sacred church into a secular mausoleum to bury distinguished citizens who shaped the nation. Over the following century, as France shifted between republics and empires, the building toggled between a church and a secular memorial, before permanently remaining a national memorial hall during the Third Republic. Entering the crypt of the Panthéon is like stepping into a living textbook of Western civilization. It houses the remains of iconic philosophers like Voltaire and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, scientists like Marie Curie (the first woman interred on her own merits) and Louis Pasteur, political heroes like Victor Schoelcher (who abolished slavery in France) and Jean Moulin (a key WWII Resistance leader), and literary titans like Victor Hugo and Émile Zola In 2002, the Panthéon welcomed one of France's most beloved writers: Alexandre Dumas (author of The Count of Monte Cristo and The Three Musketeers ), marking the 200th anniversary of his birth. President Jacques Chirac ordered his remains moved from his hometown cemetery to the national monument. However, this decision sparked considerable public controversy. Critics argued that Dumas was primarily a writer of popular entertainment rather than a serious political or moral thinker. More importantly, historians highlighted the underlying racial bias Dumas faced during his lifetime as a man of mixed race (his grandmother was an enslaved Afro-Caribbean woman). Opponents of the move questioned whether France was using him to parade racial inclusivity without confronting historic racism, while supporters celebrated his entry as a overdue victory against the prejudice that had demeaned his literary genius throughout the 19th century. Today, Dumas rests alongside his close friend and rival, Victor Hugo, bringing full circle the story of French literature.

chapters.title: The History of Firearms: From Black Powder Tubes to Modern Assault Rifles
chapters.title_zh: 火器的历史：从黑火药管到现代突击步枪
chapters.subtitle: 枪械发展史：从黑火药竹筒到现代小口径突击步枪
chapters.body: The evolution of firearms spans nearly a thousand years, marking humanity's technological leap from primitive black powder weapons to modern high-precision, automatic firearms. This history reflects advances in metallurgy, chemistry, precision manufacturing, and military tactics. 1. 枪械的雏形与早期火绳时代 (Early Firearms) 突火枪 (Fire Lance / Tu Huo Qiang): Invented in 13th-century Song Dynasty China, the Tu Huo Qiang is widely considered the earliest ancestor of firearms. Made of bamboo tubes packed with black powder and pellets (Cipao ), it used ignited gunpowder to shoot projectiles over short distances. 火绳枪 (Matchlock Musket): Developed in 15th-century Europe, the matchlock was the first shoulder-fired firearm with a mechanical trigger mechanism. A slow-burning match rope (slow match) was held by a serpentine mechanism and pulled down into a priming pan upon pressing the trigger. While a huge step forward, it performed poorly in wind and rain. 2. 燧发时代与定装弹药革新 (Flintlock & Breech-Loading) 燧发枪 (Flintlock Musket): Invented in the early 17th century, the flintlock replaced the burning match rope with a piece of flint struck against a steel frizzen to produce sparks. It dominated global battlefields for over two centuries due to its reliability and weather resistance. 金属定装枪弹与后装枪 (Metallic Cartridge & Breech-Loading): During the 19th century, two massive revolutions occurred: Metallic Cartridges: Integrated the primer, gunpowder, and bullet inside a single brass casing, making loading weather-tight, rapid, and uniform. Breech-Loading (后装枪): Replacing muzzle-loading (front loading), loading bullets into the rear (breech) of the barrel allowed soldiers to reload quickly while lying prone. 3. 无烟火药与栓动步枪黄金时代 (Smokeless Powder & Bolt-Action) 无烟火药 (Smokeless Powder): Invented by Paul Vieille in 1884 (Poudre B), nitrocellulose-based smokeless powder burned far cleaner, produced dramatically higher gas pressures, and eliminated thick battlefield smoke screens. It enabled smaller caliber bullets to travel at unprecedented velocities. 栓动式步枪 (Bolt-Action Rifle): Leveraging smokeless powder and internal magazines, bolt-action rifles became standard infantry weapons in WWI and WWII. Iconic rifles included the German Gewehr 98 / Kar98k, British Lee-Enfield, and Russian Mosin-Nagant 4. 连发武器与速射革新 (Machine Guns & Submachine Guns) 加特林机枪 (Gatling Gun): Invented by Richard Gatling during the American Civil War (1861), it featured multiple rotating barrels cranked by hand, capable of firing hundreds of rounds per minute. 机枪 (Maxim Machine Gun): Hiram Maxim invented the first fully automatic machine gun (1884), utilizing recoil energy to automatically extract, eject, feed, and fire cartridges. It radically altered infantry defense tactics. 冲锋枪 (Submachine Gun / SMG): Chambered in pistol-caliber rounds (e.g., 9mm Parabellum), SMGs like the German MP40 and American Thompson provided devastating rapid fire at close ranges during WWII. 5. 半自动、自动步枪与小口径突击步枪 (Assault Rifles) 半自动步枪 (Semi-Automatic Rifle): Fired one shot per trigger pull without manual bolt cycling (e.g., American M1 Garand 突击步枪与小口径革命 (Assault Rifle & Small Caliber Era): StG 44: Germany created the world's first true assault rifle, firing an intermediate cartridge (7.92×33mm Kurz ) that bridged full-power rifle rounds and pistol ammunition. AK-47: Designed by Mikhail Kalashnikov in 1947 (7.62×39mm ), famed worldwide for its extreme durability, simplicity, and reliability. M16 & Small Caliber Revolution: Designed by Eugene Stoner (5.56×45mm NATO ), the M16 pioneered small-caliber, high-velocity ammunition. Smaller rounds allowed soldiers to carry more ammunition while reducing recoil and improving control during full-automatic fire. 6. 侧枝演化：手枪的进化 (Pistols & Revolvers) 转轮手枪 (Revolver): Perfected by Samuel Colt in the 1830s, featuring a revolving cylinder holding multiple chambers behind a single barrel, offering rapid multi-shot capability. 自动手枪 (Semi-Automatic Pistol): Developed around the turn of the 20th century (e.g., Browning M1911 Luger P08 ), using detachable spring-loaded box magazines inside the grip for faster reloading and higher round capacity.

chapters.title: Qi Jiguang: The General Who Defeated Coastal Pirates and Rebuilt the Great Wall
chapters.title_zh: 戚继光：抗倭名将与长城重建者
chapters.body: Qi Jiguang (1528–1588) was one of the Ming Dynasty’s most celebrated military commanders, strategists, and engineers. Renowned for clearing China’s southeastern coast of pirate raids (Wokou ) and later fortifying the northern frontier against nomadic invasions, Qi redefined early modern Chinese warfare through rigorous discipline, innovative tactics, and pioneering firearms integration. 密云古北口镇历史文化公园，戚继光巨石雕像矗立其中威风凛凛 Statue of Qi Jiguang. Source: 北京- 北京旅游网 1. Historical Background: The Crisis of the Wokou During the 16th century (Mid-Ming Dynasty), China’s southeastern coast—spanning Zhejiang, Fujian, and Guangdong—was devastated by the Wokou (coastal pirates). The Wokou Threat Factors Military Decay: The traditional Ming hereditary military units (Weisuo ) were corrupt, undertrained, and regularly routed by pirate forces. Tactical Mismatch: The Wokou favored aggressive, close-quarters combat with Japanese katana blades (nodachi ) and quick ambush maneuvers that dismantled conventional Ming infantry formations. 2. The Qi Family Army and Tactical Innovations Assigned to Shandong and later Zhejiang in the 1550s, Qi Jiguang recognized that military reform required both fresh recruits and completely redesigned squad-level tactics. Building the "Qi Family Army" (Qi Jia Jun Qi bypassed corrupt garrison troops and recruited over 3,000 sturdy, disciplined miners and farmers from Yiwu, Zhejiang. He instituted strict military codes, transparent merit rewards, and rigorous collective conditioning. The Mandarin Duck Formation (Yuan Yang Zhen To counter the high lethal dexterity of pirate swordsmen in narrow southern terrains, Qi created the Mandarin Duck Formation —a flexible 12-person squad utilizing combined arms where every soldier fulfilled a distinct defensive or offensive role. 鸳鸯阵到底强在哪？其实有三条防线五种杀招，变化无穷_凤凰网 The Mandarin Duck Formation layout. Source: 历史- 凤凰网 Mandarin Duck Formation Structure Shields (Tengpai Two soldiers with large rattan or wooden shields absorbed arrows and blocked sword strikes. Wolf Bamboo Shoots (Langya Bang Two soldiers wielded multi-branched bamboo stalks fitted with iron tips to entangle enemy blades and obstruct charging swordfighters. Long Spears (Changqiang Four spearmen delivered deadly strikes over the bamboo barrier. Tridents/Short Weapons: Two soldiers guarded the rear and flanks, utilizing tridents or fire-lance firearms. 3. Major Victories and Coastal Pacification Between 1561 and 1567, Qi Jiguang led his army in a series of decisive, low-casualty campaigns across southeastern China. Battle of Taizhou (1561): Qi's forces engaged multiple pirate columns across Zhejiang, achieving nine consecutive victories and virtually eradicating the Wokou threat in the province. Campaigns in Fujian and Guangdong: Coordinating with naval commander Yu Dayou, Qi dismantled major pirate strongholds in coastal islands like Linjiang and Nan'ao, restoring maritime trade security. 4. Northern Frontier Defense: Rebuilding the Great Wall In 1568, the Ming court reassigned Qi Jiguang to the Jianguan northern front near Beijing to protect the capital against Mongol invasions led by Altan Khan. Qi Jiguang's Dual Legacy Structural Innovation (Watchtowers): Qi designed and constructed thousands of hollow, two-to-three-story brick and stone watchtowers Daitoulou ) along the Great Wall (including famous sections like Jushanling and Badaling). These towers served as self-contained garrisons housing troops, weapons, food, and signal beacons. Firearms & Wagon Squadrons: On the open northern plains, Qi developed mobile wagon forts equipped with cannons (Folangji cannons and matchlocks) to repel heavy cavalry charges. 5. Military Treatises and Historical Significance Qi Jiguang was also a prolific author whose military texts influenced Asian warfare for centuries: Ji Xiao Xin Shu (新书 / New Treatise on Military Efficiency A practical manual detailing squad tactics, weapon specifications, physical training, and unit discipline. Lian Bing Zhi Za (练兵实纪 / Practical Notes on Troop Training A comprehensive operational guide focusing on northern border logistics, artillery deployment, and command structures. Qi Jiguang’s strategic brilliance combined empirical observation with rigorous engineering, making him a timeless symbol of patriotism and military innovation.

quizzes.explanation_en: Qi Jiguang designed thousands of multi-story hollow watchtowers along the northern border, turning the Great Wall into an integrated, defensible garrison system.

chapters.title: Yue Fei: The Patriot General and the Legend of Unyielding Loyalty
chapters.body: Yue Fei (1103–1142) was one of ancient China’s most venerated military commanders and a national hero of the Southern Song Dynasty. Renowned for his tactical brilliance, strict discipline, and unwavering devotion to his country, Yue Fei led successful military campaigns against the invading Jurchen Jin Dynasty before meeting a tragic fate caused by court factionalism. 1. Historical Background: The Jingkang Incident and Crisis In 1127, the northern Jurchen Jin Dynasty captured the Song capital of Kaifeng, taking Emperor Huizong and Emperor Qinzong captive—an event known as the Jingkang Incident (靖康之变). The Southern Song Crisis (1127) Collapse of the North: The Song Dynasty lost control over its northern heartland, including the Yellow River basin. Southern Relocation: Emperor Gaozong re-established the dynasty in Lin'an (modern-day Hangzhou), forming the Southern Song Dynasty, while constantly fleeing Jurchen cavalry incursions. 2. Tattoo of Loyalty: "Serve the Country with Utmost Loyalty" According to popular historical tradition, before Yue Fei left to join the army, his mother used a needle to tattoo four Chinese characters onto his back: 精忠报国 Jīng Zhōng Bào Guó — "Serve the Country with Utmost Loyalty"). The Moral Core of Yue Fei │ 精 忠 报 国 │ This tattoo came to symbolize Yue Fei’s lifelong ethos, serving as an enduring icon of patriotism and personal integrity throughout Chinese history. 3. The Yue Family Army and Counter-Offensives Yue Fei organized and led the Yue Family Army Yue Jia Jun ), which became the main defense force of the Southern Song realm. Strict Discipline: Yue Fei famously maintained a strict moral code: "Freeze to death rather than tear down a civilian's house; starve to death rather than plunder." Anti-Cavalry Tactics: The Jin cavalry relied heavily on armor-clad heavy cavalry formations known as Iron Pagodas Tie Fu Tu ). Yue Fei countered them by arming infantry with long-handled battleaxes (Madao ) and spears to strike at the unprotected legs of enemy horses. The Northern Expeditions: In 1140, Yue Fei launched a series of successful counter-offensives, crushing Jin forces at the Battle of Yancheng and advancing near the former capital of Kaifeng. 4. Court Factionalism and Tragic Execution As Yue Fei prepared to liberate Kaifeng, deep political divisions inside the Southern Song court cut his campaign short. Political Rift in the Song Court 12 Golden Plaques: Emperor Gaozong and Chancellor Qin Hui feared that a complete military victory might restore the captive Emperor Qinzong to the throne, threatening Gaozong’s legitimacy. They issued 12 Golden Plaques (urgent imperial directives) ordering Yue Fei to abort his offensive and return to the capital. The "Mo Xu You" Charge: In 1141, Yue Fei was imprisoned under fabricated charges of treason. When questioned about the evidence against Yue Fei, Qin Hui famously replied that the charges were "Mo Xu You" (莫须有 — "Perhaps there is, or perhaps not" / "Unnecessary to prove"). Martyrdom (1142): Yue Fei was executed in Dali Temple at the age of 39, along with his eldest son Yue Yun and lieutenant Zhang Xian. 5. Legacy and Posthumous Rehabilitation In 1162, Emperor Xiaozong officially exonerated Yue Fei, restoring his honors and granting him a state burial. Yue Fei Temple: A magnificent tomb complex was erected in Hangzhou near West Lake. In front of Yue Fei’s tomb stand iron statues of Qin Hui and his accomplices kneeling in perpetual repentance. Cultural Impact: Yue Fei is celebrated in literature, opera, and martial arts tradition. The famous patriotic poem Man Jiang Hong River of Red

quizzes.question: Why did the Southern Song court order Yue Fei to withdraw despite his military victories

options.text: The army ran completely out of food and arrows.
The peace faction feared a total victory would threaten Emperor Gaozong's political power.
Yue Fei requested permission to retire early.

quizzes.explanation_en: Emperor Gaozong and Qin Hui favored appeasement and feared that reclaiming the north would return the former captured emperor Qinzong, destabilizing Gaozong's rule.

quizzes.question: How did Yue Fei's infantry defeat the Jin Dynasty's heavy cavalry

options.text: By targeting the unprotected legs of enemy horses with specialized weapons.
By building deep moats filled with water.

quizzes.explanation_en: Yue Fei used infantry equipped with long-handled axes and spears to strike at the lower legs of the heavily armored cavalry horses.

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? Yue Fei was executed immediately after losing a major battle against Jurchen forces at Yancheng.
quizzes.explanation_en: Yue Fei won the Battle of Yancheng; he was recalled while victorious and executed on fabricated treason charges by court rivals.

chapters.title: Yu Qian: The Patriot Who Saved the Ming Dynasty
chapters.title_zh: 于谦：救大明的爱国英雄
chapters.body: Yu Qian (1398–1457) was a prominent statesman, military strategist, and national hero of the Ming Dynasty. Celebrated alongside Yue Fei and Zhang Cangshui as one of the "Three Heroes of West Lake," Yu Qian single-handedly stabilized a crumbling empire during the Tumu Crisis, orchestrating the successful Defense of Beijing and preserving the continuity of Chinese civilization. 1. Early Life and the Metaphor of "Lime" Born in Qiantang (modern Hangzhou), Yu Qian passed the imperial civil service examination (Jinshi ) in 1421. Throughout his administrative career across Shanxi and Henan, he was widely revered for his incorruptibility and devotion to public welfare. Yu Qian's Personal Philosophy When visiting the capital, officials customarily presented lavish bribes to powerful court eunuchs. Yu Qian consistently arrived empty-handed, declaring that he brought only the "fresh breeze in his sleeves"—giving rise to the Chinese idiom 两袖清风 Liǎng Xiù Qīng Fēng — "having clean hands"). As a youth, he authored his famous poem Praise to Lime Shí Huī Yín ), which foretold his tragic and noble destiny: Thousands of hammer blows and chisel strikes hew it from the deep mountains; It views burning in the fierce fire as nothing out of the ordinary. Unfearing of being smashed to powder and bones broken to dust, It seeks only to leave its purity behind in the human realm. 2. The Tumu Crisis: An Empire on the Brink In August 1449, the Ming Dynasty faced an existential disaster known as the Tumu Crisis (土木堡之变). The Tumu Crisis Breakdown (1449) Disastrous Campaign: Instigated by the corrupt eunuch Wang Zhen, Emperor Zhengtong personally led an ill-prepared military expedition against Esen Taishi, leader of the Oirat Mongols. The Annihilation: The Ming army was ambushed and annihilated at Tumu Fortress. The Emperor was captured alive, and the elite guard of the imperial military perished overnight. The Factional Rift: Panic seized the capital. Some senior ministers proposed abandoning Beijing and moving the seat of government south to Nanjing—mirroring the tragic retreat of the Song Dynasty centuries earlier. 3. The Defense of Beijing: "He Who Advocates Retreat Shall Be Executed" Rising to the position of Minister of War, Yu Qian forcefully rejected the retreat proposals in court, declaring: "Those who advocate retreating to the South should be executed!" Yu Qian's Defense Strategy Constitutional Maneuver: To negate Esen Taishi's political leverage in using the captive emperor as a bargaining chip, Yu Qian persuaded the imperial court to elevate the Emperor's brother, Zhu Qiyu (Emperor Jingdi), to the throne. Desperate Mobilization: Yu Qian requisitioned grain supplies from granaries across northern China, drafted local militias, and reorganized defense lines around Beijing's nine city gates. No-Retreat Orders: In October 1449, as Oirat forces reached the outskirts of Beijing, Yu Qian led troops outside Desheng Gate and ordered the gates locked behind them. He issued a strict martial code: "If troops retreat without their commander's order, the rear line shall execute the front line." After days of intense hand-to-hand combat and artillery bombardment, the Oirat forces were repulsed, saving Beijing and preventing the collapse of the Ming Dynasty. 4. The Coup and Tragic Martyrdom Having failed to extort the Ming court, Esen Taishi released the former Emperor Zhengtong in 1450. The retired emperor was placed under house arrest for seven years by his reigning brother. Political Downfall & Rehabilitation The Restoration Coup (1457): Opportunistic court officials executed a night coup (Duo Men Zhi Bian ), reinstating Emperor Zhengtong to the throne. Fabricated Treason: Political rivals, including Xu Youzhen and Shi Heng, falsely accused Yu Qian of treason. When the Emperor hesitated due to Yu Qian's historic merit, Xu Youzhen argued: "If Yu Qian is not executed, your restoration lacks legal justification." Execution: On February 16, 1457, Yu Qian was executed outside Chongwen Gate. When investigators raided his home, they found no riches or hidden treasures—only books and imperial garments bestowed by the previous emperor. Emperor Xianzong officially exonerated Yu Qian years later, granting him the posthumous title Duansu (端肃 — "Upright and Solemn"). Today, his tomb stands near Hangzhou's West Lake, revered as a monument to selflessness and moral fortitude.

quizzes.question: How did Yu Qian eliminate the political leverage of the Oirat Mongols holding Emperor Zhengtong hostage

options.text: He paid a massive ransom using gold from the imperial treasury.
He persuaded the court to enthrone the captured emperor's brother, Emperor Jingdi.
He launched a raid to rescue the emperor from the enemy camp.

quizzes.explanation_en: By crowning Zhu Qiyu as Emperor Jingdi, Yu Qian turned the captured former emperor into a "retired emperor" without executive power, rendering Mongol ransom demands useless.

quizzes.question: What did investigators find when searching Yu Qian's home following his execution

options.text: Weapons and secret plans for a military rebellion.
Thousands of ounces of stolen silver and foreign gold.
No personal wealth, only books and imperial gifts.

quizzes.explanation_en: Yu Qian lived a frugal life; when his estate was confiscated upon his execution, officials found no personal riches.

quizzes.question: Is the following statement true? During the Tumu Crisis, Yu Qian supported moving the Ming capital south to Nanjing to avoid military confrontation.
quizzes.explanation_en: Yu Qian strongly opposed fleeing south, famously threatening to execute anyone who advocated abandoning Beijing.
